title: Trade and honesty
hook: the honest merchant is with the prophets (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, inheritance in practice, and your line: a third by will. The family's shares are fixed; the third is for the ones the shares don't reach. Whose name came to mind? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

A market in Medina. Grain is heaped up for sale, dry and golden on top. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is walking past, and instead of just looking, he pushes his hand down into the pile. His fingers come out wet. Underneath, the grain is damp. He asks the seller what this is. The man says the rain got to it. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, so people can see it? And he says: whoever cheats is not of me. A hand in a heap of grain. Today: trade, and the one thing the market can't run without.
screen: `A HEAP OF GRAIN IN MEDINA.` → `A HAND PUSHED INSIDE.` → `WET UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: In these texts the market isn't a dirty place. Tradition says the Prophet himself worked in trade before his mission, and the Qur'an mentions the caravans of winter and summer without embarrassment. What it watches is the scale. Surah eighty-three opens, in Pickthall's words, "Woe unto the defrauders," and goes on to describe people who demand full measure when they buy and give short measure when they sell. Then the reward side. In a report in Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. Sit with that company for a moment. Someone who sells phone cases, or tomatoes, or used cars, standing alongside prophets and martyrs, for nothing more dramatic than telling the truth about the goods. Next, a report in Sahih al-Bukhari makes it practical. Buyer and seller, the Prophet says, keep the right to back out until they part. If both speak truly and make things clear, their sale is blessed. If they hide things and lie, the blessing of the sale is wiped out. Notice the two verbs: speak truly, and make clear. Not lying is the first half. The second half is the grain story: showing the flaw before the buyer finds it. That is why the fiqh books give buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect the seller didn't mention. Honesty isn't left to the seller's mood. The law builds it into the contract. And so the honest merchant is not a saint who wandered into a market. It is someone who puts the wet grain on top.
screen: `THE MARKET IS NOT A DIRTY PLACE.` · `WOE UNTO THE DEFRAUDERS.` · `WITH THE PROPHETS AND THE MARTYRS.` · `SPEAK TRULY, AND MAKE IT CLEAR.`

segments.voice: Think of the last thing you sold, traded or recommended. A couch online, an old phone, a pitch at work, even a review you left. Replay it slowly. Did you say what was true? Did you also show what was wrong with it, before anyone had to find out? No grading, just looking. Now think of one sale or exchange coming up this week. Decide now which flaw you'll mention first. If you pray, you can ask for honesty in it. The bell holds the time.
Trade and honesty. In Islam, trade is honorable, and a sale is blessed when both sides speak truly and make the flaws clear. Today's word.

Your line: the honest merchant. Today, in one sale, swap or favor, put the wet grain on top: say the flaw before it's found. Tomorrow, the one kind of gain the Qur'an forbids outright. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslim merchants are taught to disclose defects, give full measure and avoid false oaths in selling, and Islamic law gives buyers a right to return goods with a hidden defect.

original.note: Arabic: truthfulness; the quality of the truthful merchant.

trapdoor: what you thought: an honest seller is one who doesn't lie.
what it means: one who speaks truly and also makes the flaws clear.
what a scholar hears: khiyar al-majlis and khiyar al-'ayb, the buyer's options, from the report in Bukhari.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 2079 (speak truly and make clear)
Qur'an 106:2 (the caravans of winter and summer)

notes: Pickthall 83:1: confirm exact wording ('Woe unto the defrauders').
Tirmidhi 1209: confirm number and wording (truthful, trustworthy merchant with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs); grading discussed by scholars.
Bukhari 2079: confirm number; paraphrase of Hakim ibn Hizam's report.
Muslim 102: confirm number and details (rain, 'put it on top', 'whoever cheats is not of me').
'The Prophet worked in trade before his mission' is from the sira (Khadijah's caravan), not cited here; Keeper may want a source or a 'tradition says'.
Right to return goods with a hidden defect (khiyar al-'ayb): confirm general framing across schools.

Editor: 'Islam never treats the market as a dirty place' softened to what the texts show; the uncited 'merchants and caravans' line now points to surah 106 (added to sources); hook close varied from the range's repeated 'Today is about...'.
